Chapter 1

Chapter 1: Introduction to Endocrinology

1.1 Hormones Action

Hormones are signaling molecules that traffic information from one cell to another, typically through a soluble medium like the extracellular fluid. Classic endocrine glands include organs like the pituitary gland, thyroid gland, parathyroid glands, pancreatic islets, adrenal glands, ovaries, and testes. It is now clear that hormones can be produced from nontraditional endocrine organs and play critical roles in the regulation of physiological homeostasis. Examples of the latter include the heart (natriuretic peptides), kidney (erythropoietin and renin), adipose tissue (leptin and adiponectin), and gut (cholecystokinin and incretins). Once in the circulation, hormones bind to receptors on target tissues to elicit their biological effects. Hormones produced in one tissue may promote activity in a target tissue at some distance from the point of secretion (endocrine effects). In this case, the hormone travels through the bloodstream, often bound to a plasma protein, to access the target tissue. In addition, hormones may act locally following secretion, either on a neighboring non-hormone-producing cell (paracrine effect), on the secretory cell itself (autocrine effect), or without actually being released from the secretory cell (intracrine effect).

1.2 The Chemical Composition of Hormones

Hormones vary widely in terms of their chemical composition: proteins (e.g., adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)), peptide hormones (e.g., growth hormone (GH), parathyroid hormone (PTH), insulin, posterior pituitary hormones), glycoproteins hormones (e.g., follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), β-human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)), © Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2020 I. monoamines (e.g., norepinephrine), amino acid derivates (e.g., thyroid hormones), steroid hormones (e.g., cortisol, aldosterone, dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), estradiol, progesterone, testosterone), lipids (e.g., prostaglandins) and signal through a variety of general (e.g., nuclear vs. cell surface) and specific (e.g., tyrosine kinase vs. phosphoinositide turnover) mechanisms in target cells. In general, protein, peptide, monoamines, and lipophilic hormones tend to exert their effect primarily through protein receptors at the cell membrane (G-protein-coupled receptors and the enzyme-linked receptors), while steroids, thyroid hormone, and vitamin D tend to operate binding to receptors found in the cytoplasmic or nuclear compartments.

1.3 Regulation of Hormone Levels

Hormone levels can be modulated through regulatory factors affecting several steps. However, the bulk of the acute “fine tuning” of hormone levels occurs at the level of hormone secretion and synthesis. Many, if not most, hormone levels are controlled either directly or indirectly by the biologic activity that they serve to control. For example, PTH secretion, which responds to low extracellular calcium levels, mobilizes calcium out of bone which, in turn, signals back to the parathyroid gland to turn off additional PTH secretion. This negative feedback loop is a hallmark of endocrine regulation. The end-product or negative regulator can either be an inorganic ion or a metabolite (e.g., calcium for PTH) or a hormonal product in the endocrine cascade (e.g., thyroid hormone for TSH, IGF-1 for GH, cortisol for ACTH), since many hormones are linked to the hypothalamus-pituitary (HP)-axis. The hypothalamus modulates hypophysis function and consequently, hormones that are produced in the pituitary gland (ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH) increase the production of hormones in peripheral glands (cortisol, T3 and T4, testosterone/estradiol, respectively). In turn, production of HP hormones is subject to negative regulation by peripheral hormones in classic feedback (FB) loops.

• Long FB refers to the hormone that was released from the peripheral endocrine

glands inhibiting pituitary and/or hypothalamic hormone secretion (e.g., IGF-1 inhibits GHRH and GH, cortisol inhibits ACTH and CRH; see Fig. 1.1).

• Short FB refers to a pituitary hormone providing negative feedback to the hypothalamus, inhibiting the secretion of the releasing hormone (e.g., GHRH is inhibited by GH, CRH is inhibited by ACTH; see Fig. 1.1).

• Ultrashort FB refers to a hypothalamic hormone that inhibits its own secretion

(e.g., GHRH, CRH). Not all feedback is negative in nature. Positive feedback loops (e.g., mid-cycle estradiol-induced LH secretion) also play important roles in governing physiological homeostasis.

Classification of Endocrine Disorders

Endocrine disorders can be classified as central (secondary or tertiary) or primary (peripheral), for those diseases affecting endocrine glands controlled by the HP axis. For instance, primary hypothyroidism refers to thyroid gland failure, while central hypothyroidism refers to TSH deficiency causing thyroid hormone insufficiency. Particular types of endocrine disorder are hormone-resistance syndromes (e.g., steroid, androgen or thyroid hormone receptor resistance syndromes). These syndromes are characterized by a clinical phenotype suggesting hormone deficiency, by ↑ levels of circulating hormone ligand and ↑ (or inappropriately detectable) levels of the relevant trophic regulatory hormone (e.g., ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH).

Chapter 2: Endocrine Hypothalamus

The hypothalamus and pituitary gland form a unit that exerts control over the function of several endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenals, and gonads), as well as a wide range of physiologic activities. The anatomic relationships between the pituitary and the main nuclei of the hypothalamus are shown in Fig. 2.1. The hypothalamus is anatomically and functionally related to the pituitary gland (hypophysis) by the infundibulum (or pituitary stalk), which consists of the hypophyseal portal system and also carries the axons of neurons whose cell bodies reside in the supraoptic nucleus (SON) and paraventricular nucleus (PVN) of the hypothalamus. The relationship between the adenohypophysis (the anterior pituitary) and the main nuclei of the HPT allows control of the anterior pituitary function by the hypothalamic hypophysiotropic hormones secreted into the portal hypophyseal vessels. The endocrine hypothalamus is organized into the:

• Magnocellular system → Neurohormones

• Parvocellular and Arcuate system → Hypophysiotropic hormones

Besides its endocrine role, the hypothalamus is involved in many nonendocrine functions such as regulation of body temperature, thirst, and food intake and is connected with many other parts of the nervous system. Hence, the hypothalamic hormones can be divided into those secreted by the neurohypophysis directly into the general circulation (neurohormones) and those secreted into hypophysial portal blood vessels (hypophysiotropic hormones). The former are synthesized in the magnocellular neurons in the SON and PVN and includes vasopressin or antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and oxytocin (both are nonapeptides). The neurosecretory granules with ADH and oxytocin travel down the long axons through the stalk to the posterior hypophysis where the granules are

The posterior lobe of the pituitary (neurohypophysis) is made up of the endings of neurons whose cell bodies reside in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. The hypophysiotropic hormones that regulate the secretion of anterior pituitary hormones include growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), somatostatin, dopamine, thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), and gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) (see Table 2.1). Most of the anterior pituitary hormones are controlled by stimulatory hormones, but GH and especially prolactin (PRL) are also regulated by inhibitory hormones. Some hypophysiotropic hormones are multifunctional. The hormones of the hypothalamus are secreted episodically and not continuously, and in some cases, there is an underlying circadian rhythm.

Physiologic Puberty

Puberty is best considered as one stage in the continuing process of growth and development that begins during gestation and continues until the end of reproductive life. After an interval of childhood quiescence—the juvenile pause—the hypothalamic pulse generator increases activity in the peripubertal period, just before the physical changes of puberty commence. This leads to increased secretion of pituitary gonadotropins and, subsequently, gonadal sex steroids that bring about secondary sexual development, the pubertal growth spurt, and fertility. The normal age at onset of puberty for girls: 8–13 years and for boys: 9–14 years. It is not clear what triggers the onset of puberty, but stimuli from the cerebral cortex and limbic system via various neurotransmitters, for example, leptin, kisspeptin, endorphins, catecholamines, GABA, and dopamine are invoked in the process.

• The physical changes associated with puberty in females include:

–– Breast development (thelarche) = the first noted sign of puberty, pubic hair development, adrenarche (the secretion of adrenal androgens), menarche –– Development of internal and external genitalia –– Pubertal growth spurt, bone mass acquisition –– Gynoid body fat disposition

• The physical changes associated with puberty in males include:

–– An increase in the size of the testes to more than 2.5 cm in the longest diameter or a testicular volume of 4 mL or more = the first sign of normal puberty –– Development of internal and external genitalia

2.2 Precocious Puberty

Precocious puberty (PP) is defined by the appearance of secondary sexual development before the age of 9 years in boys, and 7–8 years in Caucasian girls (6–8 years in African American girls).

2.2.1 Classification

1. Central (complete or true) precocious puberty (CPP) → the cause is premature

activation of the HP axis (spermatogenesis in ♂ and ovulation in ♀ may occur and fertility is possible) (the secondary sexual development is according to genetic sex).

2. Incomplete precocious puberty → premature sexual development in the absence

of HP axis maturation (without gametogenesis!)

(a) Incomplete isosexual precocious puberty (the secondary sexual development is according to genetic sex)

♂: ←excess of hCG or LH secreted by tumors  ←excess of androgens: e.g., 21-hydroxylase deficiency, 11 β hydroxylase deficiency, tumors, testotoxicosis ♀ ←a source of excessive estrogens: McCune Albright syndrome, ovarian tumors/follicular cysts

(b) Incomplete contrasexual precocious puberty

♂ ←excess of estrogens which leads to inappropriate feminization: e.g., estrogen-­secreting tumors ♀ ←excess of androgens with inappropriate virilization: e.g., congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) (e.g., 21-hydroxylase deficiency, 11 β hydroxylase deficiency)

2.2 Precocious Puberty

2.2.2 Central (Complete or True) Precocious Puberty

2.2.2.1 Etiology of CPP

9

• Constitutional (there is a familial tendency towards early puberty)

• Central nervous system (CNS) disorders such as tumors, infectious or granulomatous conditions might trigger pathologic precocious puberty

• Idiopathic (in the absence of CNS abnormality, no family history)—more common in girls

2.2.2.2 Clinical Features

1. Precocious development of secondary sexual characteristics, internal and external genitalia

(a) ♀: at least B2 (Tanner)

(b) ♂: at least G2 (testicular enlargement) (Tanner)

(c) and/or pubic—axillary hair: P2 in both sexes

2. Increased somatic development, an increase in growth velocity and skeletal maturation; when unchecked, this rapid epiphyseal development may lead to tall

stature during the early phases of the disorder but short final stature because of early epiphysial fusion!! Note: This is the paradox of the tall child growing up to become a short adult!!

3. Psychical manifestations

4. Others manifestations according to etiology

2.2.2.3 Investigations

Diagnosis of central precocious puberty has always been challenging in clinical practice.

1. Lab tests:

Serum gonadotropins and sex steroid concentrations and response to GnRH or GnRH agonists are usually similar to those found in normal pubertal subjects:

(a) Basal estradiol, FSL and LH: into the pubertal range (basal LH > 0.3 U/L

indicates the onset of puberty) The diagnostic test = GnRH stimulation test: stimulation with 100 μg GnRH (IV) or GnRH agonist (SC) → ↑LH (especially), FSH (pubertal response).

Note: The LH increase after GnRH is used as a diagnostic test to differentiate central precocious puberty from the prepubertal state.

2. Radiographs (of left wrist and hand) for determination of bone age → advanced

3. Ultrasonography of the ovary and uterus: increased uterine size, developing

4. Cerebral MRI with contrast or CT scanning (to rule out a CNS tumor/other

pathologic processes)—mandatory in all boys and girls < the age of 6

2.2.2.4 Treatment (of CPP Either Idiopathic or Due to a CNS Lesion)

Objectives: to suppress sexual maturation and decrease growth rate and skeletal maturation GnRH agonists: chronic administration of highly potent and long-acting and long-acting analogs of GnRH has been shown to downregulate GnRH receptors and reduce pituitary gland response to GnRH, thereby causing decreased secretion of FSH and LH and sex steroids and rapidly stopping the progression of signs of sexual precocity

• Triptorelin (DIPHERELINE®) 3.75 mg/vial—1 f/month (intramuscular)

• Other depot preparations: every 3 months/implantable pellets left in place for

1–2 years

2.3 Delayed Puberty or Absent Puberty (Sexual Infantilism)

Definition: Any girl of 13 or boy of 14 years of age without signs of pubertal development falls more than 2.5 DS above the mean is considered to have delayed puberty. Classification of delayed puberty

1. Constitutional delay in growth and adolescence

2. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (defects of the HP axis)

(a) Kallmann syndrome

(b) Multiple pituitary hormone deficiencies

(c) Tumors, trauma, irradiation, congenital disorders of the hypothalamus or

pituitary

3. Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism

(a) Klinefelter syndrome/other forms of primary testicular failure/anorchia or

cryptorchidism

(b) Turner syndrome/other forms of primary ovarian failure

Note: The challenging task for the examining physician is to decide which patients are constitutionally delayed and which have an organic disease.

Delayed Puberty or Absent Puberty (Sexual Infantilism)

11

2.3.1 Constitutional Delay in Growth and Adolescence

Definition: A patient with delayed onset of secondary sexual development, whose stature is shorter than that of age-matched peers but who consistently maintains a normal growth velocity for bone age and whose skeletal development is delayed more than 2 standard deviation (SD) from the mean, is likely to have a constitutional delay in puberty. Characteristics:

• More common in boys than girls

• The subject is usually thin as well; adrenarche is reported to be delayed along

with gonadarche

• A family history (a similar pattern of development in a parent or sibling)

• LH response to exogenous GnRH or GnRH agonist is pubertal

Treatment: observation/reassurance and psychological support
